title: Math anxiety: Between being able and daring to try
author: Paul Kirschner
summary: Kirschner takes on the common assumption that math anxiety is simply a symptom of low ability. Drawing on a large meta-analysis, he shows the anxiety-achievement relationship is reciprocal: anxiety depresses performance and failure feeds anxiety. He explains the cognitive mechanism, in which anxious thoughts consume working memory needed for solving problems. He rejects both the build-confidence-first and the just-practise-more answers, arguing that teachers must build competence in ways that create safety and success together. His proposed tool is low-stakes retrieval practice, framed as learning rather than judgment, with short, predictable, frequent quizzes and explanation attached. The column is a translated Dutch piece, but its pedagogical argument is clear and actionable.
points: The anxiety-achievement link runs both ways, so labeling anxious students as weak or unmotivated misreads a changeable situation.
Anxious thoughts compete for working memory, meaning an anxious child may know more than they can show.
Neither confidence-first nor drill-only works; competence and safety have to be built together through small steps and visible success.
Low-stakes retrieval practice reduces anxiety by freeing working memory, giving realistic self-knowledge, normalising mistakes and producing success.
quotes: But arithmetic or mathematics anxiety is not a character trait that is almost impossible to change, nor is it a fixed measure of aptitude. The anxiety arises in situations such as an unexpected turn to answer, a timed problem, a test, or sometimes merely the sight of a page full of symbols.

These thoughts compete for the same limited space needed to hold intermediate steps, choose procedures and retrieve knowledge from long-term memory. So a child may know more than he or she can show at that moment.

Equally simple and wrong is: “Just practise more, then the anxiety will disappear.” The art is to do both at the same time: to build competence in a way that organises safety and experiences of success (see Rosenshine: small steps and letting students experience success).
Start the lesson, for example, with three short questions on previous material. Let students first try individually, then compare, and end with good feedback.

Anxiety often lives off vagueness: “I don’t understand any of this” becomes more manageable when it turns out to be: “I mainly forget step two in equations”. Third, it normalises making mistakes (to err is human and everyone makes mistakes), provided the teacher clearly positions the exercise as learning, not assessment.
Practice tests work better when they are predictable, short, frequent and have hardly any consequences, or none at all (in fact, no-stakes). Build up from simple to more complex questions.
We cannot talk the emotion away, but we can design lessons in which knowledge is successfully retrieved more often, mistakes become information, and competence grows.
